opus-5.5.text:
I think what's beautiful is that they're really two faces of the same thing. There's this old idea in logic, the Curry–Howard correspondence, which says that a proof is a program and a proposition is a type. When you write a proof in a language like Lean, you're literally writing code, and the compiler checks whether your reasoning holds together. So proof generation isn't a separate world from code generation. It's code generation where the bar for correctness is absolute.

That matters for AI. With ordinary code, a model can write something that looks plausible, passes a few tests, and still hides a bug. With formal proofs, there's no "looks plausible." Either the proof checks or it doesn't. That gives you a perfect verifier, which is exactly what you want for training reasoning systems. The model can try things, fail, get a clean signal, and improve, without a human grading every step.

It goes the other way too. Once you can generate proofs, you can generate code that comes with a proof that it does what it claims. Today we mostly trust software because we tested it a lot. Imagine trusting it because it's been proven correct. That's huge for critical infrastructure, cryptography, compilers, anything where a bug is really expensive.

As a mathematician, the part that moves me most is that mathematics stops being purely a craft passed down in seminars and becomes something you can build on, almost like an open-source codebase. Every verified theorem is a library function someone else can call. You get compounding. Bringing code and proof together means mathematical discovery can scale the way software has, while keeping the rigor that makes mathematics mathematics. To me, that combination of creativity and certainty is the beautiful part.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what's beautiful is that they turn out to be the same problem wearing two different outfits.

When you write a proof in a language like Lean, you're really writing a program. The type checker is your compiler. If the proof type-checks, the theorem is true, full stop. There's no reviewer saying "I think this step looks fine." The machine either accepts it or it doesn't. So proof generation is code generation where correctness is built into the artifact itself.

And then you go the other direction. Most code people write has no such guarantee. You test it, you read it, you hope. But the moment you ask a model to generate code together with a specification of what that code is supposed to do, and a proof that it meets that specification, you've collapsed the gap between "it runs" and "it's right." The code becomes something you can trust the way you trust a theorem.

What I love about that is the feedback loop it creates for the models themselves. In most of machine learning you need humans to label what's good. Here the verifier is the label. A model can propose a thousand candidates, and the checker tells you instantly which ones are real. That's a training signal that doesn't lie and doesn't get tired. It's one of the few places where you can scale search and get genuine truth out the other end, rather than something that merely sounds plausible.

And there's an aesthetic side too. Mathematicians have always said a good proof should feel like it explains why something is true, not just that it's true. Good code has the same quality. When you put them together, the artifact you end up with is readable, executable, and certified. It's rare in engineering to get all three at once. To me that feels less like a tool and more like a new way of thinking.

astra-6.text:
What I find beautiful is that you’re bringing creativity and rigor into the same process. With code generation, you’re asking, “Can we build something that does this?” With proof generation, you’re asking, “Can we establish that it actually does what we intended?” And those questions can inform each other. Trying to prove a program correct can reveal a missing assumption, or suggest a simpler way to write it.

There’s also something elegant about making the specification explicit. A proof doesn’t tell you that you asked the right question, but it can give you a precise connection between what you asked for and what you built. To me, that’s the exciting possibility: generating not just a plausible solution, but a solution with a checkable argument behind it.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find beautiful is that you’re bringing together creativity and rigor. With code generation, you can explore: here’s a possible solution, here’s another way to express it. With proof generation, you ask, “Does this actually do what we intended?” And that question can guide the creative process itself.

The specification becomes a bridge between the two. You generate a program, try to prove it correct, and discover that you’ve missed an edge case—or that you haven’t quite articulated what you wanted. So you refine both your solution and your understanding of the problem.

There’s something very elegant about that loop: using reasoning to make creation more reliable, while using creation to give reasoning something concrete to work with.
